summaries.example: Imagine six clubs voting on how to spend money. One club alone cannot decide the result. But several clubs together may have enough votes to choose an outcome. Each club may also like some outcomes better than others. This is a game in the mathematical sense: players make choices, and those choices lead to an outcome.
summaries.summary: The entry explains how mathematical logic can help us reason about power in games. A game has players, possible outcomes, what each player prefers, and what each player or group can achieve. In cooperative games, groups can join together and try to move from one outcome to another. In non-cooperative games, each player chooses a strategy, often without changing choices together with the others. The entry introduces logical languages for talking about these ideas. It also explains that different questions need different kinds of logic. A language that describes group power may not be able to describe every detail of individual strategies or the timing of decisions.
key_ideas: Games can describe voting, teamwork, animal behavior, and many other situations.
Players may prefer some outcomes over others, and different players may have different preferences.
A person may have little power alone but much more power as part of a coalition.
Logic helps describe what players can do, what they want, and which outcomes are stable.
The best description depends on what we want to study. A simple language may be enough for one question, while a richer one may be needed for another.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often make decisions with others. Understanding power can help us see why a single person, a small group, or a large coalition can influence a result. Logic gives us a careful way to separate what someone wants from what they can actually do. It can also show why an outcome is stable, or why a group might be able and willing to replace it.

important_terms.definition: A carefully described situation in which players make choices and the choices lead to one or more possible results.
A possible result of the players’ choices, such as “yes,” “no,” or a certain amount of money spent.
What a person or group is able to make happen or prevent in a game.
A group of players that work together for a purpose.
A way to describe patterns using symbols and rules, so we can check what follows from them.

questions_to_think_about: Can a group be powerful even when none of its members is powerful alone?
What makes an outcome fair or stable in a voting game?
Why might two players prefer the same result for different reasons?
When would we need to describe the order in which choices happen?

summaries.example: Consider a council in which each member chooses a budget independently and at the same time. The voting rule determines which budget, if any, becomes the outcome. Preferences rank the possible budgets for each member, while an effectivity function records which sets of outcomes a coalition can force or exclude. A budget is in the core when no coalition is both able to obtain an alternative and unanimous in strictly preferring that alternative. This differs from a Nash equilibrium: there, no individual can improve by changing their strategy while the other players’ strategies remain fixed.
summaries.summary: The entry studies formal languages for reasoning about power in cooperative and non-cooperative normal-form games. A game is represented using a finite set of players, a set of outcomes, individual preference relations, and relations describing what individuals or coalitions can achieve. Effectivity functions provide an abstract account of coalitional power: they associate each coalition with sets of outcomes it can force or rule out. Coalition Logic represents such ability with operators indexed by coalitions and can characterize important structural properties of effectivity functions. For cooperative games, the core contains outcomes immune to deviations by coalitions that are both capable and willing to obtain a unanimously better alternative. For non-cooperative games, strategies and an outcome function are explicit; the principal stability notion is Nash equilibrium, where no player benefits from a unilateral deviation. Basic Coalition Logic cannot fully express Nash equilibrium because it does not retain enough information about strategy profiles and best responses. The entry surveys extensions that increase expressive power, including logics for injective games, conditional ability, quantified coalitions, stochastic outcomes, bounded resources, dynamic changes, and propositional control. Its central methodological conclusion is that no single language is universally best: the appropriate formalism depends on which features of interaction matter.
key_ideas: A normal-form game abstracts from the sequence of decisions: players choose independently and concurrently, and an outcome function maps their strategy profile to an outcome.
Preferences and abilities are distinct. Knowing what a player wants does not by itself show that the player can bring it about.
Effectivity functions model coalitional power. Their closure under supersets captures the idea that being able to ensure a narrower set also means being able to ensure any wider set containing it.
Coalition Logic expresses what groups can achieve, but its expressive resources may be too weak to define concepts requiring detailed strategy profiles, especially Nash equilibrium.
The core concerns collective deviations, whereas Nash equilibrium concerns unilateral deviations from a fixed strategy profile.
Extensions add expressive resources for quantifying over coalitions, probabilities, resource limits, conditional power, changing abilities, and control of propositions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction between preference and power prevents a common mistake: assuming that wanting an outcome is enough to secure it. Formal models also clarify different notions of stability and show exactly what information a logical language can express. This matters in the analysis of voting, collective choice, automated agents, and strategic interaction. It also explains why adding detail—such as timing, information, probabilities, or resources—can change which logic is appropriate.

important_terms.definition: A mathematical structure representing players, possible outcomes, preference relations, and action or power relations.
A relation that represents how one player ranks outcomes, including strict preference and indifference.
A function describing which sets of outcomes a coalition can force the result to remain within, thereby excluding the complementary outcomes.
A logical language using operators for relations, such as preference or coalition ability, to express properties of game structures.
The set of outcomes that no coalition can successfully challenge by obtaining an alternative that all its members strictly prefer.
A strategy profile at which no individual player prefers any unilateral change, given that the other players keep their strategies.
A condition in which a player or coalition can guarantee an objective despite the choices of opponents.
The principle that the suitable level of description depends on the features one is trying to analyze.

questions_to_think_about: Why should the core and Nash equilibrium be treated as different stability concepts?
What information is lost when several distinct strategy profiles produce the same outcome?
Why might a language that is sufficient for voting power fail to express sequential reasoning?
How do resource bounds or probabilities change the meaning of coalition ability?
When is a more detailed model preferable to a simpler one?

summaries.example: Suppose a student council must choose a fundraising plan. Each student representative votes at the same time, and the rules say that a large enough group can pass a plan. One representative may like Plan A best but be unable to pass it alone. A coalition of representatives might be able to pass Plan B, but only if all of them prefer it to the current plan. The current plan is stable if no such able-and-willing coalition exists. That idea is different from a Nash equilibrium, which asks whether any one representative would benefit by changing only their own vote while everyone else keeps theirs.
summaries.summary: The entry asks how logic can describe power in games. Games are mathematical models of players, possible outcomes, and the choices that connect players to outcomes. Each player has preferences, while individuals and coalitions have different abilities to influence what happens. The entry focuses on cooperative and non-cooperative games in which choices are made independently and concurrently. In cooperative games, the core collects outcomes that no coalition can successfully challenge with a better achievable result. In non-cooperative games, players have strategies, and a Nash equilibrium is a situation where no individual benefits from changing their own strategy while the others stay fixed. The entry explains that modal and coalition logics can represent many of these ideas, but not all of them at once. Some systems are extended to discuss resources, chance, conditional abilities, changing powers, or propositions controlled by players. The main lesson is that the right logical language depends on the question being asked.
key_ideas: A game model includes players, outcomes, preferences, and available actions or abilities.
Choices may be independent and made at the same time, so the model does not automatically describe a sequence of moves.
Coalitions can have abilities that their members do not have separately.
The core studies whether a coalition can challenge an outcome; Nash equilibrium studies whether an individual can profit by changing their own strategy.
Coalition Logic uses special operators to say that a coalition can bring about a condition.
A logical system may express some features of a game clearly while leaving other features invisible.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about power helps us distinguish influence from preference. A person may strongly want a result but lack the votes or choices needed to obtain it. These models also help explain why “stable” can mean different things: an outcome may resist group challenges but still allow one person to want a different strategy, or the reverse. Logic makes these differences precise and easier to examine.

important_terms.definition: A mathematical model of people or groups making choices that produce one of several possible results.
A ranking or comparison showing which results a player likes more, likes less, or considers equally good.
The ability of a player or coalition to make the result stay inside a chosen set of possibilities.
A group of players that coordinates its choices or interests.
A rule-based symbolic language used to describe relationships and test whether certain statements follow.
The set of results that cannot be replaced by an alternative that some coalition can achieve and all its members prefer.
A group of strategies in which no single player would do better by changing only their own strategy.

questions_to_think_about: Why can a coalition have more power than any member has alone?
How could two outcomes be equally good for one player but not for another?
Why does a Nash equilibrium not always mean that everyone is happy?
What extra information would be needed to study decisions made one after another?
Would a simple voting model or a detailed strategy model be better for analyzing a school election?
